newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania starts debates on a tough budget.
newsitem.headline: Romania starts debates on a tough budget.

text.p: Romania's new government on Thursday presented its 1997 budget, vital to reforms, with ministers forecasting a contraction in the economy but standing by previous inflation figures despite a record leap in prices last month.

Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara presented the budget to a long-awaited joint session of parliament, with the outcome of debates critical to whether Romania secures fresh international financing to underpin its reforms.

"The main aims were to scrap hidden state spending, to achieve a tolerable deficit... and to take account of social welfare," Ciumara told the assembly, dominated by the centrists who ousted ex-communists in last November's election.

Ciumara said the economy was expected to contract by three percent this year after 4.1 percent growth in 1996. But he hoped there was scope for a recovery from June once inflation was brought under control for good.

An International Monetary Fund mission is in Bucharest ahead of a decision on restoring Romania's credits at an IMF Board meeting this month. Under emergency rules, the pro-government majority is likely to approve it late next week.
The budget provides for the consolidated budget deficit to be trimmed to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from 5.8 percent last year -- nearly three times over target.
Budget indicators had been agreed during talks with the IMF and the Fund's chief representative said passage of the budget was vital to ensure its renewed support.

Ciumara stood by a 90 percent year-on-year inflation forecast despite figures this week revealing a record 30.7 percent rise in March. That sent first quarter inflation to 76.5 percent, far above a previous estimate of 41 percent.
Analysts said the forecast was out of reach and said relaxing policies could undermine an already fragile economy.
"The budget will definitely be subject to a revision this summer," independent analyst Ilie Serbanescu said. "No one can venture to make any forecast for inflation right now."

The new government has repeatedly said there is no alternative to reforms, acknowledged to have been slow under the former leftist administration, leaving Romania well behind other ex-communist countries.
"It has been proved that shock therapy, no matter how tough, bears fruit in two or three years," Ciumara said.
"We had to choose between changing the course of this country or maintaining a lukewarm situation for a short time."

Ciumara said the government inherited a dismal situation with banks hit by overdue loans, utilities deep in arrears, irrational prices and the leu currency artificially propped up ahead of last November's election.
Opposition leaders said the draft showed the government could not ensure growth and development but pledged not to block its passage in the national interest.
Adrian Nastase, Executive President of the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), said recent results showed "the inadequate nature of shock therapy for Romania's concrete conditions."
"The government must still convince parliament otherwise it would be no surprise if (the budget) were rejected," he said.
